# Gospel of Judas — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Author** | Anonymous (claiming to transmit revelation from Judas Iscariot) |
| **Date** | c. 130–170 CE |
| **Audience** | Sethian Gnostic Christians, probably in Egypt |
| **Genre** | Revelatory dialogue gospel / Sethian Gnostic apocalypse |
| **Timeline** | Mid-second century; announced to the world in 2006 |
| **In One Sentence** | A Sethian Gnostic text that presents Judas Iscariot as the only disciple who truly understood Jesus — chosen above all others to release the divine spirit from its bodily prison by handing Jesus over to be crucified. |

---

## The World Behind the Text

In 2006, the National Geographic Society announced the publication of a Coptic codex containing the Gospel of Judas — a text that Irenaeus of Lyon had described and condemned as heretical around 180 CE, which meant it had been known to exist but lost for approximately 1,800 years. The manuscript (Codex Tchacos, named for the antiquities dealer Frieda Nussberger-Tchacos through whose hands it passed) is in terrible condition — badly damaged by improper handling and storage over several decades of circulation on the antiquities black market — and its contents are accordingly fragmentary. What can be read, however, is extraordinary.

The codex was discovered somewhere in Middle Egypt in the 1970s (the exact location and circumstances are unknown — it was never a controlled archaeological excavation), and it passed through various hands in Geneva and New York over two decades before a Swiss conservation foundation (the Maecenas Foundation) funded its stabilization and translation. The dramatic and sometimes contentious story of the manuscript's modern history — including allegations of forgery, disputes over scholarly access, and competing translations — is itself a significant episode in the sociology of ancient manuscript scholarship.

The Coptic text is a translation of a Greek original that scholars generally date to roughly 130–170 CE. The Sethian Gnostic framework within which it operates — a cosmos created by ignorant cosmic beings (archons), with a supreme transcendent God above all, and the figure of Seth as the prototype of the spiritual human being — is consistent with other Sethian texts found at Nag Hammadi (the Apocryphon of John, the Three Steles of Seth, Zostrianos, Marsanes).

---

## Why This Book Was Written

The Gospel of Judas was written to rehabilitate Judas Iscariot — and to use that rehabilitation as a vehicle for a particular Sethian Gnostic reading of the meaning of Jesus's death. In the canonical gospels, Judas is the betrayer: his act of handing over Jesus to the authorities is presented as motivated by greed (Matthew, John) or satanic possession (Luke, John), and his subsequent remorse and suicide mark him as damned. He is the symbol of ultimate faithlessness.

The Gospel of Judas inverts this completely. Here, Judas is the only one of the twelve who truly understands who Jesus is. While the other disciples remain trapped in the worship of the demiurge — the inferior cosmic creator who is not the true God — Judas alone recognizes Jesus as the messenger of the transcendent realm, the "holy generation" from which Judas himself originates. Jesus takes Judas aside and instructs him secretly for several days, giving him cosmological knowledge that the others cannot receive.

The climax of Jesus's teaching to Judas is the famous passage: "You will sacrifice the man that bears me." Jesus's body is not his true self — his true self is the divine spirit within, which the body imprisons. Judas, by handing over the body to death, will be performing an act of liberation: freeing the divine from its material prison. This is salvation by crucifixion reinterpreted as the destruction of the body, not as atoning sacrifice. Judas is not a traitor — he is the greatest of the disciples, the one trusted with the most difficult task.

This inversion of the Judas tradition served several purposes. It demonstrated that Sethian Gnostics could read the canonical Gospel story and find within it a meaning opposite to the one the mainstream church derived. It articulated a soteriology in which the body and its death are the problem rather than the solution. And it positioned the Sethian Gnostics as the true insiders — the holy generation — against whom the twelve apostles and their institutional heirs were not merely deficient but actively wrong.

---

## How to Read This Book

The Gospel of Judas is shorter than it might appear — the actual text, minus scholarly introductions, is only a few dozen pages — but its fragmentary state means that significant portions of the cosmological discourse are missing or barely legible. Read it in three stages.

The opening scene sets the dramatic context: Jesus laughs at the disciples worshipping before an altar (in what appears to be a vision of the Eucharistic practice of proto-orthodox Christianity — the author is satirizing mainstream church worship as idolatry of the wrong God). Jesus questions them: "What are you doing?" They defend themselves. He tells them that what they are doing honors not his Father but a different God entirely. This is a remarkable passage: the mainstream church's Eucharist is presented as the worship of the demiurge, not the supreme God.

The private instruction sections — where Jesus takes Judas aside and begins teaching him about the cosmological system — are the theological heart. Read the cosmology carefully: Barbelo (the first emanation of the invisible God), the luminaries, the rulers (archons), the human beings created by Nebro and Saklas (hostile demiurgic powers) — all of this maps onto the Sethian cosmological system developed in the Apocryphon of John. The Gospel of Judas presupposes this system rather than explaining it from scratch, which means readers new to Sethian Gnosticism will find it dense.

The famous passage about Judas sacrificing "the man that bears me" should be read with care. There is scholarly debate about whether the text presents this as ultimately good for Judas. Recent re-examination of the Coptic by April DeConick and others has argued that the first translations (done hastily under commercial pressure before the 2006 announcement) made Judas look too heroic — in particular, that a Coptic phrase rendered "you will be greater than all of them" might actually mean "you will be cursed" or "set apart from the holy generation" — in other words, not exalted but damned. This debate is ongoing and important: the text may be more ambivalent about Judas than the initial translations suggested.

---

## The Threads — How This Book Connects

The Gospel of Judas connects most directly to the Apocryphon of John, the fundamental Sethian Gnostic cosmological text also found at Nag Hammadi. Both texts presuppose the same cosmic drama: a supreme invisible God (the Invisible Spirit), emanations from the divine pleroma, the fall of a cosmic figure that results in the creation of the material world by inferior beings, and the human being as a site of contest between the divine spark (pneuma) and the material prison. Reading the Apocryphon of John alongside the Gospel of Judas is essential for understanding Judas's cosmological teachings.

Irenaeus's description of the Gospel of Judas in Against Heresies (1.31.1), written around 180 CE, confirms the text's antiquity and its early mainstream condemnation: "They declare that Judas the traitor was thoroughly acquainted with these things, and that he alone, knowing the truth as no others did, accomplished the mystery of the betrayal." Irenaeus is our earliest external witness.

The text's presentation of Jesus laughing at the disciples is theologically significant and connects to a broader Gnostic tradition in which the earthly Jesus sometimes laughs — specifically at those who are trying to crucify his body while being unaware that his true self is beyond their reach. This "laughing Jesus" appears also in the Second Treatise of the Great Seth (another Nag Hammadi text), where Jesus says: "I was rejoicing in the height over all the wealth of the archons and the offspring of their error ... and I was laughing at their ignorance."

The rehabilitation of Judas connects, in the modern period, to Jorge Luis Borges's story "Three Versions of Judas" (1944), which imaginatively proposed similar ideas, and to the broader modern reconsideration of Judas in theology and literature. Borges was not working from the Gospel of Judas (it was unknown to scholarship at the time), but he arrived at some strikingly parallel conclusions by pure philosophical reasoning.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

The most important thing to understand about the Gospel of Judas is what it says about mainstream Christianity — not just what it says about Judas. The opening scene, where Jesus laughs at the disciples doing what appears to be celebrating the Eucharist before an altar, is an attack on the institutional proto-orthodox church. The twelve apostles represent, in Sethian Gnostic typology, the spiritual dead-ends — the leaders of a church that worships the wrong God and mistakes the demiurge's world for divine reality. This is not a friendly critique from within — it is a frontal assault on the legitimacy of apostolic Christianity.

The Sethian cosmological system is not self-evident to modern readers. The "holy generation" that Judas belongs to is the generation of Seth — the third son of Adam in Genesis, who in Sethian Gnostic theology becomes the prototype of all spiritual human beings, the ancestor of those who carry the divine spark. The "generation of Adam" and the "generation of the stars" are the lower categories of human beings. This taxonomy explains why Judas is treated differently from the other disciples — he belongs to a different ontological category.

The scholarly dispute over the correct translation of key Coptic passages is not merely academic. If DeConick's reading is correct — if Judas is actually being told he is cursed, not exalted — then the Gospel of Judas may not be a rehabilitation of Judas at all, but a Sethian text using the Judas story to dramatize the spiritual danger of serving the demiurge's purposes, even unknowingly. In this reading, the text is almost as harsh on Judas as the canonical tradition is, simply for different theological reasons.

---

## Why This Book Isn't in Your Bible

The Gospel of Judas was never a candidate for the canon. Irenaeus condemned it explicitly in 180 CE, and the proto-orthodox mainstream had been systematically excluding Sethian Gnostic texts since the second century. The document's cosmology (supreme God above the creator God), its soteriology (liberation from matter, not forgiveness of moral transgression), and its attack on the twelve apostles as worshippers of the wrong God were all incompatible with proto-orthodox theology at every level.

The text was, as Irenaeus confirms, known in some circles in the second century. But it was not widely circulated — its preservation in a single Coptic manuscript in Egypt suggests it was a marginal text even within Gnostic Christianity. The copy in Codex Tchacos was made in the fourth century, roughly the time when Bishop Athanasius was issuing canonical decrees, and it may have been concealed or abandoned around that time.

The 2006 publication generated enormous popular interest — the National Geographic announcement was front-page news globally — partly because "Judas rehabilitated" made a compelling story, and partly because the timing (Holy Week 2006) was deliberately chosen for maximum impact. Subsequent scholarly work, including DeConick's critical re-examination of the first translations, has considerably complicated the initial popular narrative.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|------|-------|
| c. 130–170 CE | Gospel of Judas composed in Greek |
| c. 180 CE | Irenaeus of Lyon describes and condemns it in Against Heresies |
| c. 300–350 CE | Coptic translation made; bound into what becomes Codex Tchacos |
| c. 1970s CE | Manuscript discovered somewhere in Middle Egypt (exact circumstances unknown) |
| c. 1983 CE | Codex appears in Geneva antiquities market |
| 1983–2000 CE | Manuscript deteriorates significantly during storage and handling |
| 2000 CE | Frieda Nussberger-Tchacos acquires codex; donates to Maecenas Foundation |
| 2001–2004 CE | Conservation and preliminary translation by Rodolphe Kasser and Gregor Wurst |
| April 2006 CE | National Geographic announces publication; worldwide media coverage |
| 2007 CE | April DeConick publishes critical re-examination of translation errors |
| 2008–present | Ongoing scholarly debate about translation and interpretation |

---
